tagline: A workflow is a **deterministic script** that orchestrates **model-driven agents** — the control flow is code, the work is still Claude.
summary: The **Workflow tool** runs a JavaScript script that fans work out across many subagents. The split is the whole idea: the **script** decides the control flow — what runs in parallel, what pipelines, how many times to loop — **deterministically**, while each spawned **agent** stays model-driven inside its step. So `agent()`, `parallel()`, and `pipeline()` are not prompts; they are **orchestration primitives** the script calls. Workflows are **opt-in** — Claude doesn't reach for one unless you ask.

sections.heading: Two layers, two kinds of decision
body: Driving the model directly, **Claude decides the fan-out** turn by turn: whether to spawn an agent, how many, in what order. That is flexible but **non-deterministic** — re-run it and the shape can change.

A workflow moves the shape into a **script**. `parallel()` is a barrier that runs thunks at once and waits for all of them; `pipeline()` streams each item through every stage with **no barrier between stages**; `agent()` spawns one subagent and returns its result. The script's loops and conditionals are **plain code** — they run the same way every time. Only what happens *inside* each `agent()` call is left to the model.

sections.heading: Why encode the orchestration
body: Three reasons a script beats ad-hoc spawning: **scale** (fan out to tens or hundreds of agents a single context could never hold), **structure** (a verify stage that adversarially checks every finding before it's trusted), and **repeatability** (the same script plus the same inputs runs the same way).

The agents still do model work — reading, judging, writing — but the **harness around them is deterministic**. You can read each phase's result and decide the next phase, staying in the loop between fan-outs.

sections.heading: Opt-in by design
body: Workflows can spawn **dozens of agents** and burn a lot of tokens, so Claude treats them as **explicit opt-in** — you ask for one ("use a workflow", "fan out agents"), or a skill invokes it. Running `/workflows` shows live progress of the runs.
This is the inverse of normal delegation: with the **Agent tool** Claude decides when to delegate; with the Workflow tool **you** decide to orchestrate, and the script decides the rest.

diagram.caption: The **script** is deterministic orchestration; the **agents** inside each step stay model-driven. Control flow is code; the work is Claude.

nodes.label: You ask for a workflow
nodes.note: Workflows are **opt-in**. Claude runs one only when you ask for orchestration or a skill invokes it — not on its own initiative.

nodes.label: Workflow script (JS)
nodes.note: A JavaScript script calling **orchestration primitives** — agent(), parallel(), pipeline(), loops, conditionals. This layer is **deterministic**: same script + same input, same shape.

nodes.label: parallel() / pipeline() fan-out
nodes.note: The script decides the shape: **parallel()** is a barrier (run all, await all); **pipeline()** streams items through stages with no barrier between them.

nodes.label: agent() spawns subagents
nodes.note: Each agent() call spawns one **model-driven subagent** with its own fresh context. The script controls *when* and *how many*; the model controls *what happens inside*.

nodes.label: Collect & synthesize results
nodes.note: Agents return structured results to the script, which filters, dedupes, or verifies them — **plain code**, not a model call — before the next phase.

nodes.label: Workflow returns
nodes.note: The orchestrated result comes back. Run **/workflows** to watch progress live across the fan-out.

scenarios.title: Fan out a review across many files **deterministically**
scenarios.note: The script's pipeline() shape is fixed; only each reviewer agent's judgement is model-driven. Re-running spawns the **same structure** of work.

scenarios.title: Loop a discovery phase until it stops finding things
scenarios.note: The **loop is in the script** — a while-condition in plain code. The agents inside each round are still Claude; the stopping rule is deterministic.

misconceptions.myth: A workflow is just a saved prompt or a macro.
misconceptions.reality: A workflow is a **JavaScript script** that calls orchestration primitives. It runs real control flow — parallel(), pipeline(), loops — not a stored block of text.
misconceptions.why: "Workflow" sounds like a saved recipe. Here it's executable orchestration code, and the agents it spawns do the open-ended work.

misconceptions.myth: The model decides the fan-out inside a workflow.
misconceptions.reality: The **script** decides the fan-out — how many agents, in parallel or pipelined, how many rounds. The model only decides what happens **inside** each agent() call.
misconceptions.why: Outside a workflow, Claude does choose when to spawn agents. A workflow deliberately moves that choice into deterministic code — that's the entire point of it.

misconceptions.myth: Claude will spin up a workflow whenever a task looks parallelizable.
misconceptions.reality: Workflows are **opt-in**. Because one can spawn dozens of agents and spend heavily, Claude runs a workflow only when you explicitly ask or a skill invokes it.
misconceptions.why: Other delegation (the Agent tool) is Claude's call, so it's natural to assume orchestration is too. The cost profile makes workflows the exception.
